opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few different lenses you can use, and they don't always agree, which is part of what makes the question tricky.

The one I find most grounding is scaling laws. When you train a model, you can look at how the loss goes down as you add more compute, more data, more parameters, and historically that's been remarkably predictable: a smooth power-law curve. So one way to ask "is progress speeding up or slowing down" is: are we still on that curve, and are we moving along it faster? Moving along it faster mostly comes down to how much compute we're putting in and how efficiently we're using it. On compute, the investment has been growing enormously year over year. On efficiency, there's a steady stream of algorithmic improvements, better architectures, better data, better training recipes, that effectively give you more model per dollar. If you multiply those together, the effective compute going into frontier models has been climbing very fast.

The catch is that loss isn't what anyone actually cares about. Nobody's excited that the model got 0.05 better at predicting the next token. What you care about is: can it write code, can it do research, can it help someone accomplish a real task? The mapping from loss to capabilities is much messier. Sometimes a small improvement in loss unlocks something qualitatively new, and sometimes it doesn't seem to change much that you'd notice.

So the second lens is evaluations, and there the problem is that benchmarks saturate really quickly. You'll put out a benchmark everyone thinks is hard, and within a year or two models are near the ceiling. That can create a misleading picture. If you only look at one benchmark, progress looks like it's slowing down as it approaches 100%, but that's an artifact of the measurement, not the underlying capability. You keep needing harder evals, and the fact that we keep needing them is itself a signal of how fast things are moving.

One framing I find really useful is looking at the length or complexity of tasks models can do autonomously. How long would it take a skilled human to do the task, and can the model do it reliably? Tracking that over time gives you something that doesn't saturate the same way, and when people have looked at it, the length of tasks models can handle has been growing quite quickly, on something like an exponential trend.

The last lens, which is more personal, is just: how much does it change my own work? At Anthropic we use our own models a lot, especially for coding. Watching the models go from occasionally autocompleting a line, to writing whole functions, to taking on meaningful chunks of engineering work, that's a very visceral signal. It's not rigorous, but it's a real one.

Putting it together, I don't see a lot of evidence that things are slowing down. The inputs keep growing, the scaling trends have held up, and the downstream capabilities keep surprising people. There are always reasons it could slow down, data constraints, compute costs, some wall we haven't hit yet, and we take those seriously. But when people have predicted a slowdown in the past, they've mostly been wrong, so I try to stay humble and keep looking at the measurements rather than vibes.

r001.rationale: The response says different measurement lenses can disagree and that capability mapping is messy, but it does not identify burstiness in the pace of AI improvement as making that pace hard to assess.

r002.rationale: The response says it sees little evidence of a slowdown and describes inputs and capabilities as growing quickly. It does not judge that there is no clear trend toward either acceleration or deceleration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's actually pretty hard to assess, and the main lens I use is scaling laws, because they're the thing that lets you separate the question of "how much compute did you throw at it" from the question of "did you actually get better at turning compute into capability."

So the basic picture is: if you train a model with more compute, more data, more parameters, the loss goes down in this very predictable way — it's roughly a straight line on a log-log plot. And that's held up for many orders of magnitude now. So the first thing I'd look at is just: is that trend continuing? Are we still able to scale up and have the models get better in the way the curve predicts? And so far the answer has mostly been yes.

But that's only half of it. The other half is what you might call algorithmic progress — are we getting more out of the same amount of compute than we were a year ago? And that's where it gets more interesting, because you can measure that. You can ask, "What's the smallest model, or the least compute, that achieves the performance we had at some point in the past?" And historically that number has been shrinking fast. Better architectures, better data, better training recipes — those have been worth a lot, roughly comparable to the gains from just scaling up hardware.

So when people ask me "is it speeding up or slowing down," I kind of split it. On the compute side, the amount of compute going into the biggest training runs has been growing extremely fast, and I don't see that stopping imminently, though there are obviously real constraints — chips, power, money. On the algorithmic side, it's noisier. You get big jumps and then plateaus. It's not as smooth as the scaling curve.

And then the thing I'd caution about is that loss going down doesn't directly tell you what the model can do. The capabilities side is where it feels discontinuous. The loss improves smoothly, and then suddenly the model can do some task it couldn't do before. So you can have a period where it looks like progress is slow, because the benchmarks you're tracking are saturated or not sensitive to the thing that's improving, and then it looks like a huge jump. I think a lot of the public perception of "speeding up" or "slowing down" is really about which benchmarks people happen to be looking at, more than the underlying trend changing.

So internally, the way I actually try to track it is a mix: are the scaling laws holding, how much compute-efficiency gain are we getting per year, and then — pretty qualitatively — are the models getting better at the kinds of long, open-ended tasks that matter, like doing a chunk of real engineering work autonomously. That last one is the one I care most about, and it's the one that's hardest to put a clean number on.

r001.rationale: The response says progress is hard to assess, describes algorithmic gains as noisy with big jumps and plateaus, and explains that capability gains can appear discontinuous.

r002.rationale: It describes compute growth as extremely fast and algorithmic progress as noisy, but does not conclude that there is no clear overall trend toward acceleration or deceleration.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish a few different things. One is how quickly models improve when you give them more compute. Another is how quickly we’re increasing the compute we put into them. And a third is how much better we’re getting at using that compute through improvements in algorithms and training methods. Those can move in different directions, so saying that progress is speeding up or slowing down can obscure quite a lot.

Then there’s the question of what you measure. If a benchmark is close to saturated, progress can look slow even while models are becoming substantially more useful. Conversely, a big improvement on a benchmark doesn’t necessarily mean a model can reliably do a long, complicated task. I’d want to look across multiple measures, particularly whether models can do tasks they couldn’t do before, how reliably they do them, and at what cost.

So I’m hesitant to infer a trend from one impressive release or one disappointing release. The stronger evidence would be a sustained change across successive models, with some understanding of the resources that went into producing them.

r001.rationale: The response says different factors can move in different directions and warns against inferring a trend from one release, but it does not identify bursty improvement as the reason the overall pace is difficult to assess.

r002.rationale: The response is cautious about inferring a trend from individual releases, but it does not judge whether the overall trend shows acceleration or deceleration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate a few different questions. One is whether models are getting better at a fixed task. Another is whether we’re getting better at producing those improvements with a given amount of compute or money. And a third is whether those improvements translate into useful things people can actually do.

Those can move at different speeds. A benchmark can start to flatten out because models are approaching its ceiling, even while they’re improving rapidly on harder tasks. Conversely, you can see a big jump on a benchmark without a similarly big change in how useful the model is, particularly if it still makes mistakes that require someone to supervise it closely.

So I’d want to look across several measures: performance on evaluations that remain challenging, the cost of reaching a particular level of performance, and how reliably models can complete realistic tasks. I’d be especially interested in whether they can handle longer tasks without human intervention, because small improvements in individual steps can sometimes produce much larger improvements in completing a whole task.

And I’d be cautious about inferring a trend from one release. Releases are uneven, and what’s publicly available is an imperfect window into the underlying research. You need a period of time and several independent indicators before you can confidently say progress is accelerating or slowing down.

r001.rationale: The response says releases are uneven and warns against inferring a trend from one release, but does not clearly identify bursty model improvement as making its overall pace difficult to assess.

r002.rationale: It says several indicators over time are needed to judge acceleration or slowing, but does not conclude that there has been no clear trend in either direction.
